prompt: Develop a preliminary solar-water-heating plan for a residential building with 40 residents. Present exactly five workflow steps. Cover demand assessment, key components and connections, seasonal/backup operation, installation and maintenance risks, and performance checks. Roof area, local climate, water-use measurements and energy prices are unknown. Identify missing information and how it affects choices instead of inventing exact sizes, savings or costs. Keep the plan under 550 words.
answer:
1. **Assess demand and site feasibility.**  
   Confirm occupancy patterns for the 40 residents; measure daily hot-water use, peak draw rates, inlet temperature and required delivery temperature. Include distribution and recirculation losses. Survey usable roof area, shading, orientation, structural capacity and pipe routes. Obtain local solar-radiation, temperature and freeze data. These inputs determine feasible solar contribution, collector area and storage capacity; occupancy alone does not justify exact sizing.

2. **Choose components and map connections.**  
   Compare certified flat-plate and evacuated-tube collectors against climate, available roof area and maintenance needs. Assess indirect glycol or drainback arrangements where freezing is possible; consider direct circulation only where climate, water quality and regulations permit. Conceptual connection: collector circuit → heat exchanger/solar storage → backup heater → thermostatic mixing valve → hot-water distribution. Cold water supplies the storage system. Include appropriate pumps, sensors, insulation, isolation, expansion, pressure relief and backflow protection.

3. **Define seasonal and backup operation.**  
   Use differential-temperature control to collect useful solar heat without cooling storage unnecessarily. Size backup heating for the required service when solar input is unavailable, considering measured peaks and acceptable recovery time. Select electricity, gas or another source only after checking existing services, tariffs and constraints. Establish winter freeze protection and summer low-demand/overheating protection. Coordinate backup controls with a locally compliant hygiene-temperature regime and anti-scald delivery protection.

4. **Resolve installation and maintenance risks.**  
   Have qualified professionals verify roof loading, wind resistance, waterproof penetrations, safe maintenance access and plumbing/electrical compliance. Address leaks, corrosion, scaling, potable-water contamination, stagnation temperatures and pressure hazards. Water testing should guide material selection and scale-control provisions. Provide accessible components and a maintenance schedule covering collector condition, insulation, pumps, controls, mixing valves, relief devices and heat-transfer fluid where applicable. Identify who will maintain the system and fund replacements.

5. **Commission and verify performance.**  
   Test leaks, flow rates, sensors, controls, backup recovery, freeze/overheat safeguards, delivered temperatures and hygiene provisions. Meter hot-water demand, useful solar heat and backup energy; record weather and operating conditions so results can be compared fairly with design expectations across seasons. Investigate poor performance before expanding capacity. Obtain installed-price quotations, energy tariffs and maintenance estimates before assessing lifecycle costs or savings; report ranges and assumptions rather than unsupported exact figures.
